1.pericope_label: My son, attend unto my wisdom: for the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb

schools.summary: Henry claims prophetic inspiration for the speaker though the prophetic formula is absent, defines the genre against speculation and disputation as a guide to the government of ourselves, and holds that those mighty in the scriptures may be spiritual priests in their conversation as the priest is said to keep knowledge with his lips.

Gill reads the wisdom offered as that of a greater than Solomon, notes that two ancient versions insert matter here absent from the Hebrew, supports the honey and the wormwood from two Latin poets, and takes the descent of the sixth verse both of bodily and of eternal death.

Clarke grounds the lessons in the speaker’s own experience, keeps the balance of honey and bitterness exactly, adds a serpent whose poison infects the whole constitution, and says it is impossible to conceive all the wiles of the sixth verse, learning them being part of the science first taught in that trade; Wesley reads the same verse of a woman who transforms herself into several shapes to prevent serious consideration.

Ellicott finds the scriptural parallel to honey turning bitter in a message sweet in the mouth and bitter in the belly, traces the smooth mouth to a recorded betrayal, and sets out both readings of the sixth verse before preferring the one in which the woman’s own steps wander unobserved; Keil and Delitzsch ground the teaching in years of observation, treat bitterness and poison as one in the language, weigh the plural of the sword, and reject the reading that makes the sixth verse an address to the hearer.

debates: On what authority does the teacher speak? Keil and Delitzsch make it a father’s wisdom of life gained through many years of experience and observation, and Clarke says outright that the lessons are drawn from the speaker’s own experience; Henry claims that he writes by divine inspiration and is a prophet, though he does not use the prophetic formula.

Whose ignorance does the sixth verse describe? Clarke and Wesley take the woman’s arts to be aimed at preventing her victim from reflecting on where he is going; Ellicott gives that as the sense of the English version but prefers a rendering in which it is her own steps that wander without her observing it, and pictures her tottering on with eyes shut until she falls to rise no more; Keil and Delitzsch canvass the ways of construing the clause and reject the Jewish reading that turns the verb into an address to the hearer.
outliers: Gill quotes one Latin comic poet for honeyed words and another satirist for the saying that she has more aloes in her than honey.
Henry distinguishes this teaching from speculation and doubtful disputation, holding that its object is the government of ourselves rather than the filling of our heads with notions.
Clarke calls the endless variation of the woman’s devices a science, and the first thing taught in that trade.
themes: authority claimed from experience and from inspiration
sweetness and bitterness measured against each other
a warning aimed at conduct rather than at speculation
a crux over whether the seducer or the seduced is the one lost
devices multiplied to prevent reflection

7.pericope_label: Remove thy way far from her: and thou mourn at the last, when thy flesh and thy body are consumed

schools.summary: Gill reads the forfeited honour as wealth and reputation as well as bodily vigour, citing two versions for strength of body, urges shunning the woman as one would the pest or a loathsome carcass, hears the mourning of the eleventh verse as the roar of a lion, and holds the sorrow to be worldly rather than repentant, coming too late to be of use.

Clarke warns against the door in particular for the exhibitions about it, describes the cruelty that sits enthroned behind the blandishments and the robberies and murders that follow, and abandons philology for testimony, saying he has often been called in the line of his duty to such death-beds, where groans and shrieks were incessant; Wesley combines dignity, reputation and strength of body and mind in the forfeited honour, and calls the harlot one of the most cruel creatures in the world.

Ellicott reads the seventh verse as the point where the teacher stops quoting his father and speaks in his own person, gives flight as the safeguard all moralists advise with one mouth, renders the forfeited honour as freshness and vigour, names the cruel as the temptress or her hangers-on bent on plunder, and offers two senses of the fourteenth verse, universal sin or death by stoning; Keil and Delitzsch treat the seam as a discourse boundary, observe that the passage nowhere appeals to the criminal punishment of the adulterer, trace the word for groaning to an echo of natural sound, and canvass the same alternatives at the fourteenth verse before preferring every kind of evil.

debates: What does the fourteenth verse confess? Ellicott gives two senses, that the speaker had almost fallen into every sin and might have committed any of them openly, or that he might have been visited with the extremest punishment at the hands of the congregation, death by stoning; Keil and Delitzsch report one scholar taking the word directly of stoning and another of the totality of evil, and settle for every kind of evil while allowing the penalty may be thought of at the same time, having earlier observed that the discourse nowhere appeals to the criminal punishment of the adulterer at all.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch note that the Greek version read a different Hebrew word at the eleventh verse and rendered it thou shalt repent, and call this a happy exchange, since in a cognate tongue the two verbs mean respectively to breathe hard and to repent.

Clarke reports from his own pastoral duty that he has often been called to the death-beds of such persons, where the groans and shrieks were incessant through the pains in their bones and flesh, and says that whoever has witnessed such a scene will see with what propriety the passage is written.
Ellicott holds that flight is the great safeguard in such temptations, and that all moralists advise it with one mouth.
Clarke observes that murders have often taken place in brothels as well as robberies, since that vice is one of the parents of cruelty.
themes: a warning grounded in consequence rather than in law
distance prescribed as the only defence
youth and vigour counted as the price paid
a word for groaning that imitates its own sound
a self-sentence pronounced too late to help

15.pericope_label: Drink waters out of thine own cistern: rejoice with the wife of thy youth

schools.summary: Henry defends the prescription of marriage against the charge that God deals unkindly, since a man may not eat of every tree but may choose one and freely eat, nature being content with one and lust with nothing; he quotes a poet twice, for the maxim that man would have been the encloser had God laid all common and for the rule to abstain wholly or wed, and holds the allowed pleasures far to transcend the forbidden.

Gill reports a claim that a Greek philosopher took from the Hebrews a law about not drawing water from another man’s ground, reads the dispersed streams as children who marry and become fountains in turn, argues that a man keeping to a virtuous wife is sure the children are his own, and allegorises the section into the truths of the Gospel and the pure church set against the apostate one.

Clarke makes the counsel run both ways, the wife being required not to tempt her husband by unkindness to seek elsewhere what he cannot find at home, holds a brood born outside marriage no credit to any man, and breaks off his own note on the fountain with the rule that anatomical allusions must not be pressed into detail in a commentary; Wesley reads the streams as children, calls the word for ravished hyperbolical, and notes that excess in the marriage bed is plainly possible.

Ellicott reads the seventeenth verse of privacy rather than paternity, since the deepest joys and sorrows of a heart are sacred and strangers have no part in the relations of family life, and identifies the two animals from their grace, speed and lustrous eyes; Keil and Delitzsch press the physical terms of the figure in two learned languages, deny that the second animal is the gazelle and make it the chamois, hold moderation a duty within marriage as well as outside it, and decline the allegorical reading of the whole section.

debates: Is this section to be read allegorically? Keil and Delitzsch record that the ancients and one modern scholar so read it, and decline to follow, holding that the allegory does not remove what is sensual in the passage; Gill reads it that way throughout, making the dispersed streams the truths of the Gospel and the loving hind the pure church set against the apostate one.

What does the seventeenth verse secure? Gill, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch all take it of paternity, the last observing that a child born outside marriage belongs to no one in particular and must for his father’s honour be denied before the world; Ellicott sets generation aside and reads it of privacy, since the deepest joys and sorrows of a heart cannot be shared and strangers have no part in family life.
outliers: Clarke stops his own note on the fountain with the rule that anatomical allusions must not be pressed into detail in a commentary on scripture, at the very place where Keil and Delitzsch supply that detail at length in Latin and Greek.
Henry quotes a poet twice in one paragraph, for the maxim that if God had laid all common man would certainly have been the encloser, and for the rule to abstain wholly or else wed.
Gill reports the claim that a Greek philosopher derived from the Hebrews a law forbidding husbandmen to take water from others until they had dug in their own ground.
Wesley calls the word rendered ravished hyperbolical and observes that excess within the marriage bed is plainly possible.
themes: marriage prescribed as the cure rather than as a concession
one tree granted where all were desired
children counted as the dispersal of a household
a figure pressed by one commentator and refused by another
moderation required inside the permitted bond

21.pericope_label: For the ways of man are before the eyes of the Lord: he shall be holden with the cords of his sins

schools.summary: Gill argues from the pains men take to hide what other men would shame them for, that the certainty of divine knowledge should weigh far more, describes the adulterer’s illusion that age will weaken his lusts and leave repentance available, and offers three renderings of the last verse, as instruction justly withheld at death, as death incurred because instruction was refused, or as correction rather than teaching.

Clarke sets out the binding of the last verses as a sequence in which repeated sin becomes custom, custom engenders habit, and habit assumes the form of necessity, so that a man is bound with cords of his own making; he then accepts the closing sentence as generally true but refuses to make it absolute, holding that even such men may repent and live. Wesley glosses the same verse as dying in one’s sins and straying from the way of life.

Ellicott makes the closing argument the certainty of detection by a Judge whose eyes run through the whole earth; Keil and Delitzsch state what the verse contributes to the argument, that irregular intercourse is the commencement of a fool’s ruin, weigh whether the phrase about the eyes is adverbial or predicative, and render the last clause as staggering to ruin in the fulness of folly.

debates: What does it mean to die without instruction? Gill offers three senses, that those who rejected instruction in health should justly be denied it in dying, that the man dies because of instruction in the sense that he would not bear it, which two Jewish commentators support, or that the word means correction and amendment rather than teaching; Clarke accepts the sentence as generally true but denies it is absolute, holding that even such men may repent and live.
outliers: Clarke describes the binding as a four-stage descent, from pleasure taken at will, to custom, to habit, to necessity, at the end of which the cords are the man’s own.
Gill notes that men take great pains at concealment precisely because they would be ashamed if other men knew, and argues from that pains-taking to how much more the knowledge of God should weigh.
Gill adds that the cords may be read of guilt and punishment, since the horrors of a guilty conscience need no other officer to make the arrest.
themes: conduct argued from the certainty of being seen
an illusion that habits will loosen with age
freedom lost by degrees to one’s own repetitions
a sentence stated generally and softened in application
folly ending in a stagger rather than a fall
